paragraphs.source_en: Down-headed animals are of all dimensions, from only a few centimetres large such as that at In Itinen en haut (see figure 5-6) but more frequently of larger dimensions up to 3 m long, as at Tin Aboteka (figure 5-2). There are two types of down-headed animals, one is bulky with short legs, and the other is more slender with longer legs. When of large dimensions they are located in the central part of the wall and all the other anthropomorphic or zoomorphic figures, usually of smaller dimensions, are placed around them. Their importance in the rock art is therefore evident and they must have had a significant role in the society producing the Round Head art.

paragraphs.source_en: In order to approach a possible interpretation of this phenomenon I use a comparative study of the South African rock art. Here similar kinds of animals exist which were interpreted, on the grounds of ethnographic record, as animals of the rain (Solomon 1992; Lewis-Williams 1981; 2004). These rain animals are characteristically rounded, fat, and herbivore-like. They bear little resemblance to known species, and their form is therefore not determined by a concern for realism or naturalism. However, snakes, bovids, antelope, hippopotamuses and non-real conflations of these and other animals also fall into the category of creatures of the rain (Lewis-Williams 2004; Challis 2005).

paragraphs.source_en: The San distinguish two kinds of rain and each has its respective animal: a rain-bull is an undesired thunderstorm that destroys the people's huts; the rain-cow is the gentle, soaking rain bringing the fertility (Lewis-Williams 2004). These animals are managed by special kind of people called rain men or shamans of the rain, who interact with them. Rain men are believed to catch a rain animal beneath the water surface and to lead it through the sky to the place where the rain is needed or to the top of a nearby hill. There they cut and kill it so that its blood would fall as rain.
